accepted.s: Which of the following groups consists entirely of biodegradable agricultural and livestock wastes?
o: Cattle dung, fluorescent lamps, manure and tyres
Stubble, mercury, pesticides and dairy waste
Paddy husk, lead, manure and solvents
Crop residue, cattle dung, dairy waste and manure
accepted.x: Crop residue, manure, cattle dung and dairy waste are biodegradable agricultural or livestock wastes. Lead, mercury, solvents, pesticides and fluorescent lamps are hazardous materials.
accepted.tq: Identify the option containing only members of the same waste category.
accepted.sec: Agricultural waste - crop residue, livestock waste - uses  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: GOBARdhan primarily promotes the conversion of cattle dung and agricultural waste into
accepted.x: GOBARdhan, launched in 2018, promotes the conversion of cattle dung and agricultural waste into biogas and bio-slurry.
accepted.tq: Direct recall of a scheme and its principal output.
accepted.sec: Agricultural waste - crop residue, livestock waste - uses  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which of the following is NOT a stated use of crop residue?
accepted.x: Crop residue can be converted into pellets and briquettes, subjected to torrefaction, or co-fired in power plants. Fluorescent-lamp production is not a use of crop residue.
accepted.tq: Find the option outside the stated set of applications.
accepted.sec: Agricultural waste - crop residue, livestock waste - uses  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which one of the following is an appropriate application of agricultural waste as a biomass resource?
o: Use as feedstock for advanced biofuels
Use as a substitute for all mineral ores
accepted.x: Agricultural waste can serve as biomass feedstock for advanced biofuels. The other options do not represent the stated uses of agricultural waste.
accepted.tq: Apply the waste-to-resource concept to identify a valid use.
accepted.sec: Agricultural waste - crop residue, livestock waste - uses  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the four classic characteristics used to identify hazardous waste?
accepted.x: The four classic characteristics are ignitability, corrosivity, reactivity and toxicity. Biodegradability is not one of these four classic criteria.
accepted.tq: Reject a familiar environmental term that does not belong to the defined list.
accepted.sec: Hazardous waste - defining characteristics, household examples  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s:
Consider the following characteristics of hazardous waste:
1. Explosiveness
2. Infectiousness
3. Radioactivity
4. Corrosivity
Which of the characteristics are additionally recognised in the AP classification besides the four classic criteria?
accepted.x: The AP classification adds explosive, infectious and radioactive characteristics to the four classic criteria. Corrosivity is already one of the classic criteria and is therefore not an additional characteristic.
accepted.tq: Separate additional criteria from characteristics already included in the standard list.
accepted.sec: Hazardous waste - defining characteristics, household examples  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s:
Hazardous waste may occur in which of the following forms?
1. Solids
2. Liquids
3. Sludges
4. Gases
accepted.x: Hazardous waste can occur as solids, liquids, sludges and gases. Hence, all four forms are included.
accepted.tq: Use the all-inclusive option after verifying every item in the classification.
accepted.sec: Hazardous waste - defining characteristics, household examples  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which of the following is correctly matched as a household hazardous waste?
accepted.x: Paints and batteries are household examples of hazardous waste. The other options generally represent biodegradable or non-hazardous household wastes.
accepted.tq: Match a household item with its correct waste category.
accepted.sec: Hazardous waste - defining characteristics, household examples  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s:
Arrange the following stages of the hazardous-waste management hierarchy in the correct order from higher to lower priority:
A. Recycling
B. Prevention
C. Recovery
D. Safe disposal
accepted.x: The hierarchy places prevention above recycling, recovery and safe disposal. The relevant sequence is prevention, recycling, recovery and safe disposal.
accepted.tq: Arrange the stages by priority rather than by time of occurrence.
accepted.sec: Hazardous waste - defining characteristics, household examples  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which of the following correctly represents the complete hazardous-waste hierarchy given in the specified order?
o: Reuse, prevention, recovery, minimisation, recycling, disposal, co-processing
Minimisation, prevention, recycling, reuse, co-processing, recovery, disposal
Prevention, minimisation, reuse, recycling, recovery, co-processing, safe disposal
Prevention, recycling, minimisation, reuse, safe disposal, recovery, co-processing
accepted.x: The stated hierarchy is prevention, minimisation, reuse, recycling, recovery, co-processing and safe disposal.
accepted.tq: Recall the exact sequence in a graded management hierarchy.
accepted.sec: Hazardous waste - defining characteristics, household examples  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which statement regarding the waste hierarchy is correct?
o: Reduction at source is the top priority in the 3R approach.
Regain replaces Reduce in the standard 3R formulation.
Recycling means using an item again in its original form.
Reuse means converting waste into a different usable material.
accepted.x: Reduction at source is the top priority. Reuse means using an item again in its existing form, while recycling converts waste into other usable materials.
accepted.tq: Distinguish closely related terms by their precise meanings.
accepted.sec: Waste hierarchy - 3R/5R  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which of the following may be added in expanded 5R versions of the waste hierarchy?
accepted.x: Expanded 5R versions may add Refuse and Repurpose or, in some versions, Recover. The versions vary, but Refuse and Repurpose are stated additions.
accepted.tq: Identify the additional terms in an expanded version of a familiar list.
accepted.sec: Waste hierarchy - 3R/5R  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Every city is intended to have a permanent RRR Centre under
o: The Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules, 2016
accepted.x: Every city has a permanent RRR Centre under SBM-U 2.0. RRR is expanded in the cited context as Reduce, Reuse and Recover.
accepted.tq: Link an institutional facility with the correct mission.
accepted.sec: Waste hierarchy - 3R/5R  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Refuse-Derived Fuel is primarily produced by
o: Burning untreated wet waste in open areas
Composting only agricultural and livestock waste
Compressing radioactive waste into inert blocks
Shredding and dehydrating high-calorific municipal solid waste after removing recyclables and biodegradables
accepted.x: RDF is made by shredding and dehydrating high-calorific MSW, mainly non-recyclable plastic, paper and textiles, after recyclables and biodegradable material are removed.
accepted.tq: Identify a process from its input, treatment and output characteristics.
accepted.sec: Refuse-Derived Fuel (RDF)  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: RDF is used mainly as an alternative fuel in
o: Cement kilns and thermal power plants
accepted.x: RDF is used as an alternative fuel in cement kilns and thermal power plants.
accepted.tq: Directly connect a waste-derived product with its principal end-use.
accepted.sec: Refuse-Derived Fuel (RDF)  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding RDF:
1. It mainly contains non-recyclable plastic, paper and textiles.
2. Recyclables and biodegradable waste are removed before its preparation.
3. It is produced from high-calorific municipal solid waste.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: RDF is prepared from high-calorific MSW, particularly non-recyclable plastic, paper and textiles, after removing recyclables and biodegradable waste. All three statements are correct.
accepted.tq: Confirm the input, composition and pre-processing steps together.
accepted.sec: Refuse-Derived Fuel (RDF)  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: The Andhra Pradesh Pollution Control Board has permitted how many cement industries to co-process incinerable, plastic and municipal waste?
accepted.x: The APPCB permitted 12 cement industries to co-process incinerable, plastic and municipal waste.
accepted.tq: Recall the exact institutional count and distinguish it from nearby figures.
accepted.sec: Refuse-Derived Fuel (RDF)  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: How many pre-processing facilities feed cement plants in the RDF-related arrangement described for Andhra Pradesh?
accepted.x: Six pre-processing facilities feed cement plants in the stated arrangement.
accepted.tq: Use the smaller associated figure rather than the number of participating cement industries.
accepted.sec: Refuse-Derived Fuel (RDF)  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which agency functions as the state agency running urban sanitation under SBM-U 2.0 in Andhra Pradesh?
o: Andhra Pradesh State Council of Higher Education
accepted.x: Swachha Andhra Corporation, or SAC, is the state agency running urban sanitation under SBM-U 2.0 in Andhra Pradesh.
accepted.tq: Identify the correct state agency from closely related institutional names.
accepted.sec: AP state agency for integrated waste chain  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Swachha Andhra Corporation operationalised Project Monitoring Units for Swachh Survekshan 2026 in how many ULBs?
accepted.x: SAC operationalised Project Monitoring Units in 46 urban local bodies for Swachh Survekshan 2026.
accepted.tq: Distinguish a programme-monitoring count from the wider ULB coverage figures.
accepted.sec: AP state agency for integrated waste chain  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which statement correctly describes the Re Sustainability MoU in Andhra Pradesh?
o: It covers all 123 ULBs for scientific e-waste collection, disposal and MRFs.
It covers only 30 ULBs for rural sanitation.
It operates only the state’s WtE plants.
It tracks hazardous waste through GPS-fitted vehicles.
accepted.x: The Re Sustainability MoU covers all 123 ULBs for scientific e-waste collection, disposal and material recovery facilities. The 30-ULB figure relates to the ITC MoU.
accepted.tq: Separate similar institutional agreements by coverage and function.
accepted.sec: AP state agency for integrated waste chain  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: APEMC portal — Swachh Survekshan ranking only
CBMWTF — GPS tracking of hazardous-waste vehicles
Re Sustainability MoU — monitoring only WtE electricity generation
accepted.x: Real-time monitoring is carried out on the APCMMS portal. The APEMC portal tracks hazardous waste using GPS-fitted vehicles, while BMW is sent to CBMWTFs.
accepted.tq: Match each portal or facility with its specific operational function.
accepted.sec: AP state agency for integrated waste chain  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Biomedical waste in Andhra Pradesh is sent to Common Bio-Medical Waste Treatment Facilities primarily for
o: Production of RDF for cement kilns only
accepted.x: Biomedical waste is sent to Common Bio-Medical Waste Treatment Facilities for incineration. It is not intended for open dumping or untreated agricultural composting.
accepted.tq: Identify the prescribed treatment route for a specialised waste stream.
accepted.sec: AP state agency for integrated waste chain  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which portal tracks hazardous waste through GPS-fitted vehicles in Andhra Pradesh?
accepted.x: The APEMC portal tracks hazardous waste using GPS-fitted vehicles. APCMMS is associated with real-time monitoring.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between similar-looking portals by their exact function.
accepted.sec: AP state agency for integrated waste chain  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: The Andhra Pradesh Circular Economy and Waste Recycling Policy 2025–30 was issued through
accepted.x: The AP Circular Economy and Waste Recycling Policy 2025–30 was issued through G.O. Ms. No. 26.
accepted.tq: Recall the exact government-order number associated with the policy.
accepted.sec: AP state agency for integrated waste chain  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which of the following correctly shows the municipal solid-waste collection chain?
o: Door-to-door collection → segregated transport → transfer station → MRF → processing/recycling → residual landfill
Transfer station → door-to-door collection → landfill → MRF → recycling
Door-to-door collection → landfill → segregation → transfer station → MRF
MRF → door-to-door collection → segregated transport → landfill → processing
accepted.x: The chain begins with door-to-door collection, followed by segregated transport, transfer station, MRF, processing or recycling, and final residual landfill.
accepted.tq: Arrange a service chain by its operational sequence.
accepted.sec: Collection chain - door-to-door, segregation, transfer stations, MRFs  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: According to the cited Andhra Pradesh performance figures, what percentage of wards had full door-to-door coverage?
accepted.x: Full door-to-door coverage was reported for 94.62% of wards in the cited Andhra Pradesh figures. The 49.32% figure relates to wards with 100% source segregation.
accepted.tq: Distinguish closely related percentages by the service they measure.
accepted.sec: Collection chain - door-to-door, segregation, transfer stations, MRFs  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which of the following correctly matches the Andhra Pradesh waste-management indicators?
o: 100% source segregation in wards — 49.32%; MRFs — 101 ULBs
100% source segregation in wards — 94.62%; MRFs — 30 ULBs
accepted.x: The cited figures are 49.32% of wards with 100% source segregation and MRFs in 101 ULBs.
accepted.tq: Start from the sure percentage and verify the associated institutional count.
accepted.sec: Collection chain - door-to-door, segregation, transfer stations, MRFs  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: What was the stated target for rural door-to-door waste collection in Andhra Pradesh by March 2026?
accepted.x: The target was 100% rural door-to-door collection by March 2026. The 97% figure refers to door-to-door collection in municipalities.
accepted.tq: Separate a target from an already reported performance figure.
accepted.sec: Collection chain - door-to-door, segregation, transfer stations, MRFs  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which statement about the national gaps in municipal solid-waste management is correct?
o: All ULBs had notified SWM by-laws and 45% had achieved full segregation.
Fewer than 45% of ULBs had notified SWM by-laws and 68% had achieved full segregation.
Only 68% of ULBs had notified SWM by-laws and fewer than 45% had achieved full segregation.
68% of ULBs had notified SWM by-laws and more than 45% had achieved full segregation.
accepted.x: The cited national gaps were that only 68% of ULBs had notified solid-waste-management by-laws and fewer than 45% had achieved full segregation.
accepted.tq: Keep the two percentages attached to their correct indicators.
accepted.sec: Collection chain - door-to-door, segregation, transfer stations, MRFs  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which of the following statements regarding waste-to-energy in India is correct?
o: There are 21 WtE plants producing exactly 133 MW and no biogas facilities.
There are 133 operational WtE plants producing 21 MW, along with 170 biogas facilities.
There are 170 operational WtE plants producing 21 MW, along with 133 biogas facilities.
There are 21 operational WtE plants producing more than 170 MW, along with 133 biogas facilities.
accepted.x: The cited figures are 21 operational WtE plants producing more than 170 MW and 133 biogas facilities.
accepted.tq: Match each number with the correct category and unit.
accepted.sec: Waste-to-energy - WtE, bio-CNG, CBG  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Waste-to-energy plants are stated to reduce the volume of municipal solid waste by approximately
accepted.x: WtE is stated to reduce municipal solid-waste volume by approximately 90%.
accepted.tq: Recall the approximate quantitative effect rather than an exact unsupported value.
accepted.sec: Waste-to-energy - WtE, bio-CNG, CBG  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: The additional WtE capacity targeted under SBM-U 2.0 is
accepted.x: SBM-U 2.0 targets an additional WtE capacity of 10,000 tonnes per day.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the programme target from existing plant capacity.
accepted.sec: Waste-to-energy - WtE, bio-CNG, CBG  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which of the following correctly describes the SATAT–GOBARdhan linkage?
o: It establishes 500 new MRFs exclusively for e-waste.
It provides 500 MW from existing WtE plants only.
It targets 500 new waste-to-wealth CBG plants.
accepted.x: The SATAT and GOBARdhan linkage targets 500 new waste-to-wealth compressed biogas plants.
accepted.tq: Link two initiatives with their stated numerical target and output.
accepted.sec: Waste-to-energy - WtE, bio-CNG, CBG  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Compressed biogas plants described in the waste-to-energy context convert municipal wet waste into
accepted.x: CBG plants convert municipal wet waste into green fuel. The Circular Bioenergy Scheme supports scientific processing in this area.
accepted.tq: Infer the useful product from the waste input and technology named.
accepted.sec: Waste-to-energy - WtE, bio-CNG, CBG  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which scheme of the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas supports 100% scientific processing in the cited circular-bioenergy context?
accepted.x: The Circular Bioenergy Scheme of the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas supports 100% scientific processing in the cited context.
accepted.tq: Identify the scheme from its sector and stated purpose.
accepted.sec: Waste-to-energy - WtE, bio-CNG, CBG  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which pair of Andhra Pradesh cities is associated with WtE plants?
accepted.x: The cited Andhra Pradesh WtE plants are located at Guntur and Visakhapatnam.
accepted.tq: Recall a location pair without substituting nearby urban centres.
accepted.sec: Waste-to-energy - WtE, bio-CNG, CBG  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Legacy waste refers to
o: Agricultural residue stored for use as animal fodder
Old municipal solid waste piled in dumpsites for years
Only hazardous waste stored in laboratories
Freshly segregated waste awaiting transport for one day
accepted.x: Legacy waste is old municipal solid waste accumulated in dumpsites over several years. It can emit methane and pollute groundwater.
accepted.tq: Select the definition that captures both age and storage condition.
accepted.sec: Legacy waste - biomining and remediation  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which of the following is a consequence of accumulated legacy waste?
o: Improvement of groundwater quality without treatment
accepted.x: Legacy waste can emit methane and pollute groundwater. These impacts necessitate remediation and scientific processing.
accepted.tq: Connect a waste condition with its stated environmental consequences.
accepted.sec: Legacy waste - biomining and remediation  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Biomining of legacy waste involves
o: Burning all waste together in an uncontrolled fire
Excavating the waste and separating recyclables, RDF, bio-soil and inert fill
Converting only the biodegradable fraction into manure
Covering the dump permanently without excavation or segregation
accepted.x: Biomining involves excavation and separation of legacy waste into recyclables, RDF, bio-soil and inert fill. It is not uncontrolled burning or mere covering.
accepted.tq: Identify the complete treatment process from its stages and outputs.
accepted.sec: Legacy waste - biomining and remediation  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Under the stated SWM Rules 2026 approach, landfills should be used only for
o: Recyclable plastic and paper before sorting
All mixed municipal waste collected from cities
accepted.x: Landfills are intended only for waste that is non-recyclable, non-energy-recoverable and inert. Recoverable and recyclable materials should be diverted for processing.
accepted.tq: Use the exclusion principle to identify what may finally enter a landfill.
accepted.sec: Legacy waste - biomining and remediation  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which measure is specifically associated with the management of legacy dumpsites under the stated SWM Rules 2026 approach?
o: Mapping all legacy dumpsites and undertaking time-bound biomining or bioremediation with quarterly reporting
Allowing indefinite accumulation until the dumpsite reaches capacity
Sending all legacy waste directly to agricultural fields
Banning all reporting after the first year of remediation
accepted.x: The approach requires mapping all legacy dumpsites, time-bound biomining or bioremediation and quarterly reporting.
accepted.tq: Choose the option containing the complete compliance package rather than one isolated action.
accepted.sec: Legacy waste - biomining and remediation  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: At Guthikondavaripalem in Ongole, how much of the 2.56 lakh tonnes of legacy waste had been processed?
accepted.x: At Guthikondavaripalem, 1.76 lakh tonnes out of 2.56 lakh tonnes of legacy waste had been processed.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the processed quantity from the total quantity and the wider state estimate.
accepted.sec: Legacy waste - biomining and remediation  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: The inherited legacy waste of Andhra Pradesh was placed at approximately
accepted.x: The inherited legacy waste of Andhra Pradesh was placed at 108 lakh tonnes. This is distinct from the 2.56 lakh tonnes at the Ongole site.
accepted.tq: Handle Indian-numbering figures carefully and distinguish state totals from site-specific quantities.
accepted.sec: Legacy waste - biomining and remediation  [GROUP-II]
